Galileo’s recantation to the Roman Inquisition required him to assert that the Earth was, as the Church insisted, the centre of the universe, orbited by the Sun.

...

The younger Galileo was, as Mario Livio shows in Galileo and the Science Deniers , an eager controversialist, as able in polemics as he was in observational science. As early as 1615, he had clashed with the “Peripatetics” (Aristotelians) who governed the Church and thus controlled the accepted intellectual matrix of the time. Heliocentrism was deemed to be contrary to scripture and thus heretical. In the end, it was his personal attack on the pope, Urban VIII, that sparked his trial. Galileo’s guiding belief was that the universe spoke in the language of mathematics, while the Church believed in the absolute sufficiency of Holy Writ.
The story is more complex than usually told. While surrounded by science deniers, Galileo was himself a Galileo denier. The most unconvincing part of his defence was that he was actually trying to refute Copernicanism, the heliocentric model. Nor did he probably mutter “e pur si muove” (but still, it moves) as he was led away.
